note: Prewritten copy for the Moon / Learned / Next pages. Every item cites PSI investigations by ID (resolved to DOI links at build time) and/or the NASA Space Apps challenge brief. Experiment claims paraphrase the goal/findings/moon fields of data/experiments.json; items marked hypothesis restate a hypothesis, not a result.

moon.title: Flames on a Moon base
moon.lede: A lunar habitat will not breathe like the ISS. Exploration atmospheres carry more oxygen at lower pressure — and that changes how fire behaves.

atmospheres.name: Earth, sea level
atmospheres.note: The baseline every material test assumes.

atmospheres.name: Moon base and rovers
atmospheres.note: Over 40% more oxygen than Earth air, at about two-thirds the pressure.

sections.heading: What the PSI data already shows

items.title: Still air does not put the fire out
items.text: BRE burned gas-fed emulations of solid materials in exploration atmospheres with no airflow at all. At 26.5% oxygen and 10.2 psia, and at 34% and 8.2 psia, flames kept burning in a quasi-steady way; the same flames at 21% oxygen self-extinguished quickly. On the ISS, shutting off ventilation starves a fire. In a Moon-base atmosphere it may not.

items.title: Droplet data reaches 40% oxygen
items.text: FLEX-2 burned fuel droplets across oxygen mole fractions from 0.10 to 0.40 and pressures from 0.5 to 3.0 atm, a range that overlaps the atmospheres expected in habitats.

items.title: The highest-oxygen flames in the archive
items.text: CFI-G fed up to 85% oxygen out of a porous burner into a fuel atmosphere — the highest oxygen level in any PSI microgravity test, and the closest analogue to an oxygen-enriched habitat.

sections.heading: Partial gravity is the missing axis

items.title: No PSI investigation has burned anything at lunar or Martian gravity
items.text: The archive's flight results are all from freefall, and its ground and modelling work covers 1 g and 0 g. The Moon (0.16 g) and Mars (0.38 g) sit between those two bounds, where buoyancy is weak but not absent. Partial-gravity experiments such as LUCI and FM2 are expected to start filling the gap.

items.title: An electric field can stand in for gravity
items.text: E-FIELD Flames uses an electric field to drive an ion wind through the flame — a body force that stretches or flattens it much as buoyancy would. It is the only PSI dataset that mimics partial gravity, and can help interpolate between 0 g and 1 g.

learned.title: What we learned
learned.lede: More than two decades of fires in freefall, read for what they say about keeping a crew alive: stopping fires before they start, noticing them, and putting them out.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.intro: Which materials burn, and under what conditions.

items.title: Richer atmospheres remove a safety margin
items.text: With no airflow, flames at 21% oxygen went out on their own; in elevated-oxygen exploration atmospheres they kept burning. The result also suggests NASA's cone-calorimeter test (Test 2) could predict microgravity flammability.

items.title: Earth's upward-burn test may not be the worst case
items.text: BASS-II tests the hypothesis that ventilated materials burn as well or better in microgravity than in 1 g, which would mean the standard 1 g upward-burning screen is not conservative for space. BASS results support that hypothesis.

items.title: Slow air is what feeds a fire in orbit
items.text: Without buoyancy, low-speed flow from cabin ventilation is the dominant oxygen supply. Modelling built on BASS imagery aims to reproduce a 'Goldilocks' zone in which flames survive only in a middle range of flow speeds.

items.title: Fires were tested at realistic scale without a crew
items.text: The Saffire experiments burned large fabric sheets and samples of real spacecraft materials aboard uncrewed Cygnus vehicles after they left the ISS, to measure how fast a large fire grows and to check NASA's material-selection criteria.

sections.heading: Detection
sections.intro: What smoke looks like without gravity, and whether detectors see it.

items.title: Smoke particles may be larger in microgravity
items.text: SAME-R works from the hypothesis that microgravity smoke particles are larger and fewer per unit mass, which can stop some detectors from alarming. Post-flight tests validated its assumption that particle sizes follow a lognormal distribution.

items.title: The first attempt taught a lesson of its own
items.text: SAME's particle samples came back contaminated, which motivated the reflight; detector response was still determined from the video record.

items.title: Dust and smoke share an instrument
items.text: DAFT proved a particle counter in microgravity using dust; the same instrument later measured smoke. That overlap is the starting point for a lunar problem: dust that could set off smoke alarms.

items.title: Gravity changes how smoke grows
items.text: Simulations built on SAME data explore the hypothesis that without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer drop, changing particle growth and smoke composition.

sections.heading: Suppression
sections.intro: What it takes to put a fire out, and whether it stays out.

items.title: A baseline for choosing extinguishing agents
items.text: FLEX measured how well gaseous suppressants (carbon dioxide, helium, sulfur hexafluoride) work on burning droplets, and builds limiting-oxygen-index diagrams against pressure.

items.title: The agent the ISS already uses was tested on solids
items.text: BASS tested nitrogen as an inert gaseous extinguishing agent on thick, realistic fuels in a controlled flow.

items.title: Out is not always out
items.text: Cool flames, first observed in FLEX, can persist after the visible flame is gone. Follow-on work maps when a fire that looks extinguished may continue as a cool flame, and shows that small residual airflows decide whether cool flames survive.

next.title: What we need to do next
next.lede: The archive is deep where the ISS made testing easy and thin where a Moon base will actually operate. Four gaps stand out.

items.title: Burn something at partial gravity
items.text: No PSI investigation has run at 0.16 g or 0.38 g. Today the only handles are the 0 g and 1 g bounds, an electric-field stand-in for a body force, and smoke simulations that can be re-run at lunar or Martian gravity. Partial-gravity experiments such as LUCI and FM2 are the expected next step.

items.title: Test real solids in a Moon-base atmosphere
items.text: The elevated-oxygen results come from gas burners emulating solids and from droplets. Real solid samples were burned at or below 21% oxygen, and large-scale tests of real cabin materials ran in cabin air. Nobody in the archive has burned real materials at 30% oxygen and reduced pressure.

items.title: Tell smoke from lunar dust
items.text: Lunar dust could confuse smoke detectors. The dust-instrument data and the smoke particle-size work are a starting point, not an answer: none of the investigations here measured smoke and dust together.

items.title: Pin down the cool-flame re-ignition hazard
items.text: Cool flames can outlive the visible fire. The droplet experiments, laboratory counterflow flames and simulations describe when they appear and persist; what is missing is what that means for a real habitat fire after suppression.
